channel.title: My Azeroth Life
channel.description: Grand adventures in a reborn Azeroth: World of Warcraft: Forever stories and the occasional detour into retail.

item.title: The Lightbloom and the Knight-Errant
item.description: The candy bucket at the inn in Silvermoon City was the one honest thing in the city that night. Laotou reached in, came out with a fistful of Hallow’s End treats, and was congratulated for it as though a war had been won. Trick or Treat, the elves called it. The chronicler has seen grown heroes cheered for less, but not often.
item.content:encoded:
The candy bucket at the inn in Silvermoon City was the one honest thing in the city that night. Laotou reached in, came out with a fistful of Hallow’s End treats, and was congratulated for it as though a war had been won. Trick or Treat, the elves called it. The chronicler has seen grown heroes cheered for less, but not often.

It had been a wandering sort of evening before that. The monk began it in the Bazaar beneath the Sanctum of Light, and within a minute had a new name stitched under the old one: Azeroth Morning Radio. A guild, then. Laotou joined at the rank of Commoner, which is the most truthful rank any guild has ever handed out. Everyone starts at the bottom of the hall, sweeping. Pandaren do not mind sweeping. It is a close cousin to meditation.

From there the road went home, or near enough. Founder’s Point, up on Stoneveil Ridge, where a door opened onto a house and the monk went inside and stayed a while. The chronicler does not follow anyone through their own front door. Some pages are meant to stay blank. Some time later Laotou came back out onto the ridge, looked at the sky the way travelers do when they are deciding which obligation hurts least, and went to Dornogal.

Dornogal held the monk only briefly. Then the Wizard’s Sanctum in Stormwind, which is less a place than a door with an attitude, then Silvermoon again, and the bucket, and the treats.

Then Eversong Woods, and the work.

The Path of Dawn runs gold under the leaves, and Fairbreeze Village sits beside it like a village that has never once been told bad news. The people of Fairbreeze had their troubles ready: neighbors driven out of their homes, a beast called Sharpmaw that needed answering for, and the small favors a village asks of any stranger with strong hands and no good excuse. Laotou took all three and had all three settled before a candle could burn down. Sharpmaw has been answered for. How, exactly, was not written down.

After that the monk went deeper. Saltheril’s Haven, where the elves keep their manners polished and their cellars more so. Goldenbough Pass. And Lightbloom Ath’Ran, where something called the Lightbloom was looming, which is not a thing a flower ought to do. Laotou looked into it and came back with an answer someone was willing to pay for, and two new questions in hand. The Lightbloom wants trimming, and someone wants to know why it is growing at all. Curious cultivation, they called it. The chronicler calls it a garden that has started to get ideas.

The road south ran past Tranquil Repose, where the dead of this forest are laid down with more grace than they were shown in life, through Tranquillien, and on to the edge of Zeb’Nowa, where the Amani keep long memories and longer grudges. Then the monk turned back toward the city, as if remembering an appointment.

There was one. Knight-Errant Bloodshatter.

That name has sat on Laotou’s list since the monk first came to Silvermoon. At Astalor’s Sanctum the hunt was finally marked closed. The chronicler was not there for the end of it and will not invent a duel. What is known is what came after. A Spark of Tides was pressed into the monk’s hand, the kind of thing that hums when you hold it too close to your ear. There was a chest of the Preyhunters’ spoils, and gloves and boots of plain leather that were somehow still better than what the monk had been wearing. And there was a stole, the Preyhunter’s Rugged Stole, settled across the shoulders.

A hunter’s mantle is an odd fit for a Pandaren who spends their days keeping other people breathing. It suits Laotou anyway. Healing in this world is its own kind of hunt. You track death down before it reaches your friends.

Somewhere in all that a mask turned up too, Hallow’s End being what it is. The chronicler did not see which face it was. Perhaps that is the point of a mask.

Laotou ended the night in Silvermoon City some four hundred gold heavier, which in a city of elves is roughly the price of being looked at politely.

And already a new name has taken the old one’s place. Senior Tinker Ozwold. The hunt-masters at Astalor’s Sanctum hung it on the board, and the monk took it down. Out in Eversong the Lightbloom keeps growing, untrimmed and curious. And the letters from Khaz Algar still wait. The Weaver, The Vizier and The General are not known for patience.

item.title: Down the Darkway
item.description: The thing called Infiltrator Gulkat had made its home at the bottom of the Darkway, and like most creatures that settle at the bottom of anything, it had not expected company.
item.content:encoded:
The thing called Infiltrator Gulkat had made its home at the bottom of the Darkway, and like most creatures that settle at the bottom of anything, it had not expected company.

Burrly came anyway. He went down out of the Bazaar in Silvermoon City with Valeera Sanguinar at his shoulder, the same quiet blade who walked the Shadow Enclave with him, and the two of them descended into a passage the elves had named honestly for once. The Darkway is dark. It is also a way. Beyond that the elves offer no comfort, and the chronicler offers less.

It was slow work, measured in loose coins and broken stone. He chipped ore from the walls when the walls allowed it, pulled a stubborn weed or two from cracks where nothing should grow, and gathered small blessings off the fallen as he went: a Boon of Vigor, a Boon of Temperance, a Boon of Fortitude, and twice over a Boon of Possibilities, which is a fine name for a thing nobody can explain. Somewhere along the way he shrugged the Rampant Thornmantles off his shoulders and put on the Front-Line Shoulders of the Aurora. Front-line is about right. He has never stood anywhere else.

Then Gulkat. The chronicler was not down there and will not invent the blows. What is known is the ending. The infiltrator stayed down, and Burrly came up holding a new sword: the Exhumed Soul-Cleaver. He set aside the Enchanted Crypt Greatsword he had pulled from a tomb in Eversong only days ago and took up a blade whose very name admits it was dug out of the ground. In the last entry the chronicler wrote that the dead would one day want their things back. The Kul Tiran’s answer, it seems, is simply to keep trading up among them. Two Corrosive Souls went into his pack as well. He did not say what he means to do with them, and the chronicler did not ask.

Valeera left at the surface, as she does, without farewell. Burrly walked to the harbor, sold what the dark had given him, and went into the Bazaar to close the Delver’s Call he had carried since the last entry. Nearly four hundred gold for the trouble. Somewhere between the coin and the counter he felt it again, that quiet thickening of arm and back that comes from surviving one more thing that meant to kill him. Another rung on a ladder that never ends.

He did not rest. The hunters of Silvermoon had work, and their errands read like a sermon: Astalor’s Initiative, The Power of Anguish, When Predator Becomes Prey, To the Sanctum! He ran them back and forth between Sunstrider Isle and the harbor like a messenger carrying letters between two lovers who refuse to meet.

Then the real hunt, out along the Path of Dawn, for a man called Knight-Errant Bloodshatter. The name alone suggests someone who gave up on subtlety early. Somewhere in that chase a war supply crate came down out of the sky, because Eversong in a season of war is like that, and Burrly helped himself before anyone could argue. When it was done, Bloodshatter was finished, and the Kul Tiran walked away with an Aspiring Preyhunter’s Chest, a Spark of Tides, and the Preyhunter’s Clasp, which he hung at his throat in place of the plain Eversong Chain. Aspiring. Even the trophies in this city are condescending.

He came back to Silvermoon with two new errands in his ledger: Senior Tinker Ozwold, whom the hunters would like found, and something called Hope in the Darkest Corners, which is either a task or a sentiment this city has not felt in years.

Late that night he returned for a single minute. Coin was waiting for him, better than sixteen hundred gold of it, the long tail of everything he had sold. Then thirty-three thousand gold left his purse in one breath. Where it went, he did not say. Families keep their own ledgers, and the chronicler is not always shown them.

Ozwold is still out there. Hope is still in the darkest corners, wherever those are. And north of Eversong, the Gates of Zul’Aman are still waiting, as patient as only troll stone can be.

item.title: A Stranger in Dornogal
item.description: The first thing Laotou did in Dornogal was unroll a map that, by its own name, showed Everywhere All At Once. The second was to go and find money.
item.content:encoded:
The first thing Laotou did in Dornogal was unroll a map that, by its own name, showed Everywhere All At Once. The second was to go and find money.

Laotou is new to this ledger. A Pandaren monk out of Stormrage, arriving in Khaz Algar with the steady eyes of someone who has already done a great deal of walking somewhere the chronicler was not watching. The earthen of Dornogal had a stack of letters waiting before the monk had properly set down a pack: something called Midnight, something else on the horizon, three separate notices that The Weaver, The Vizier and The General each wanted a word, and two special assignments, What Remains of a Temple Broken and Push Back the Light. Nobody arrives in Dornogal without immediately being handed somebody else’s problems.

The monk set them aside, found five hundred gold, and then walked into the Council’s Treasury and found thirty-five thousand more.

The chronicler has been at this a long time, and gold does not fall out of the sky. In the same few minutes that night, a Kul Tiran in Silvermoon, a gnome in Eversong, an orc in the Bazaar and a young Nightborne in Orgrimmar each emptied their purses. Burrly. Tibbit. Gruffhug. Zerxie. The chronicler draws no line between those dots in ink. In pencil, perhaps.

What Laotou did with the fortune was practical, which is the most Pandaren thing imaginable. Five strongboxes in the Treasury vault, bought one after another, each dearer than the last: a hundred gold, then five hundred, a thousand, twenty-five hundred, and finally five thousand. Then nearly nine thousand gold more changed hands in Dornogal, and the monk came away with an Arcanoweave Reagent Rucksack and three Sunfire Silk Backpacks. Pandaren understand something the other races keep forgetting. Before a long road, you sort your pack.

Then the monk sat down and remembered the old disciplines. Not the fist, but the mist. Chi-Ji, the Red Crane, called down out of the sky. Restoral. Celestial Conduit. Sheilun’s Gift, named for an old staff with older stories. And Revival, the art of pulling a whole company back from the edge at once. These are not a brawler’s teachings. These are the teachings of someone who means to keep other people alive, which in Azeroth is the more thankless trade by a wide margin.

From Dornogal the monk went to Silvermoon City and the Sanctum of Light, and was handed a road called Eversong. A small welcome called Adventuring in Midnight was finished on the spot. Something on the Horizon was set down unread; the horizon will keep. Laotou took on Hope in the Darkest Corners, as everyone in that city seems to, and then the hunters’ errands: Astalor’s Initiative, The Power of Anguish, When Predator Becomes Prey, To the Sanctum! All four done before the tea could cool, back and forth between Sunstrider Isle and the harbor, a pace that suggests the monk has run errands for elves before.

The night ended in Silvermoon with a pick and a pair of shears bought from the trainers, a gold coin each, because even a healer has to eat.

There is still a name on Laotou’s list: Knight-Errant Bloodshatter. By the chronicler’s count, he has been waiting for a great many people lately. And three letters from Khaz Algar remain unanswered, from The Weaver, The Vizier and The General, none of whom are known for patience.

item.title: Parhelion Plaza
item.description: The Darkway does not announce itself. It simply opens under Silvermoon City like a throat, and the only courtesy it offers is darkness honest enough to keep its name.
item.content:encoded:
The Darkway does not announce itself. It simply opens under Silvermoon City like a throat, and the only courtesy it offers is darkness honest enough to keep its name.

Laotou went down out of the Bazaar with two Delver’s Calls still warm from the board — The Darkway and Parhelion Plaza — and Valeera Sanguinar walking at the monk’s shoulder. The chronicler has watched that blade join a great many parties. She never explains herself. She never needs to. By the time the pair reached the bottom of the passage, Laotou had already pulled weeds from cracks that should not have held life, gathered the small blessings the dark coughs up for anyone stubborn enough to keep walking — a Boon of Fortitude that shone like something the world did not mean to drop, a Thalassian Phoenix Plume still warm with old fire, a Boon of Vigor, then another — and left Infiltrator Gulkat where infiltrators belong when their work is finished.

The chronicler was not down there and will not invent the blows. What is known is the ending. Gulkat stayed down. Laotou came up wearing Miststalker’s Brigandine across the chest, a name that sits well on a Pandaren who means to keep other people breathing. Valeera left at the surface without farewell, as she does. Some companions are weather. They arrive. They pass. You do not ask them to stay.

From Silvermoon Harbor the monk crossed the Shining Span onto the Isle of Quel’Danas, where the light still pretends it won something permanent. Parhelion Plaza waited beyond — a place that sounds like a poem until you are inside it, and then it sounds like stone and hard work. Valeera rejoined without ceremony. Somewhere in that press the world flickered toward a Voidstorm and back again, the way old wounds do when the weather turns. More boons. More coin. A Boon of Possibilities twice over, which is a fine name for a thing nobody can explain and everyone pockets anyway.

Then Gladius Slaurna.

Again, the chronicler will not invent the fight. The gladius stayed down. Laotou hung a Serpentine Talisman at the throat and walked out of Parhelion Plaza with an enchanter’s formula stuffed in a pouch — Empowered Rune of Avoidance, for a helm that has not yet asked for it — and nearly eight hundred gold heavier than when the evening began. Valeera left again. The pattern holds.

Back in the Bazaar, both Delver’s Calls closed in the same breath. The coin for finishing them was honest. What came after the coin was quieter: that thickening of limb and spirit that comes of surviving one more place that meant to keep you. Laotou felt it in The Bazaar of Silvermoon City and understood, without needing anyone to say so, that the road had lengthened again. Eighty-one. Another rung on a ladder that never ends.

The night closed toward the Sanctum of Light. The letters from Khaz Algar still wait — The Weaver, The Vizier, The General — and none of them are known for patience. Parhelion Plaza is finished. The horizon is not.

item.title: The Long Road Through Tor’Watha
item.description: The unseen foe lasted about a minute.
item.content:encoded:
The unseen foe lasted about a minute.

Burrly came back to Eversong Woods among the ruined troll stones of Tor’Watha, where yesterday’s question had been waiting for him all night like a creditor on the doorstep. A Foe Unseen, the elves had called it. The chronicler had braced for a long hunt through the gold-leafed undergrowth. Instead the Kul Tiran walked into the clearing, settled the matter, and collected his fee before the ink on yesterday’s page had properly dried. Whatever had been planting those vines is a foe seen now, and that is generally the last thing such a creature gets to be.

That should have been the end of it. In Quel’Thalas, nothing is ever the end of it.

Following the Root took him deeper, because roots go somewhere and somebody always wants to know where. Gods Before Us came next, and the name alone should have warned him. The Amani raised Tor’Watha for gods who were here before the elves arrived and fully intend to be here after they leave. Burrly walked among their broken altars with the careful manners of a man who knows how little the dead care for manners. An Impasse followed, then Beat of Blood, each one a door opening onto a narrower hallway.

He changed his clothes on the way, as warriors do, without ceremony and without a mirror. The Burnt Watha’nan Breastplate went over his chest, scorched black along the edges by some fire the chronicler would rather not know the origin of. A Puzzling Crypt Relic went into his belt pouch, a trinket so named because no one, least of all Burrly, can say what it is for. And into his hands went an Enchanted Crypt Greatsword. The chronicler notes that he has spent a week in Eversong dressing himself out of the tombs of the dead. At some point the dead will want their things back.

He also found, once again, a parcel of Bazaar Bites. Two nights running now. Someone in Silvermoon is losing a great many suppers in this forest, and the chronicler is beginning to suspect it is the same someone.

Light Guide Us carried him up into Amani Pass, where the trolls once held the road against all comers and the stones still remember it. That one was a proper fight, long and grinding, the kind that leaves a man breathing hard and leaning on his sword. He came out of it changed. Not wiser, exactly. Stronger, the way the body grows stronger when it keeps surviving things it had no business surviving. An Eversong Defender’s Helm came out of the pass with him, and he set it on his head in place of the dead man’s mask he had worn out of Deatholme. The chronicler counts that a small mercy. Past Redemption was done in the same breath, and then a task called Fractured, which is how most of Quel’Thalas would describe itself if anyone thought to ask.

Then trouble on two legs found him.

The name was Urdaru, out of Wyrmrest Accord. Eversong was quiet one moment and not the next. A Blackout Kick landed like a falling mast, and the Kul Tiran met the dirt of the pass face first. The forest, which has watched elves and trolls kill each other here for four thousand years, did not look up.

So he went where the killing is at least organized.

Silvershard Mines, with a borrowed company of strangers. A hunter named Thedüde, out of Tichondrius, put an arrow in him twice, once in passing and once with real intent. Delphias added a third. Burrly kept getting up. Somewhere between the second death and the third, he and his fellows rode a mine cart from its rails all the way to the depot without ever losing their grip on it, which sounds small until you have tried it under hunter fire. The Alliance carried the field. He walked out with a fuller purse and his dignity roughly where he had left it.

He made one stop in Silvermoon City to settle accounts. Fractured, closed. The Delver’s Call for the Shadow Enclave, closed at last, with nearly four hundred gold for the trouble he and Valeera had seen down there. And a new road written into his ledger: The Gates of Zul’Aman.

Then Warsong Gulch, because a man killed four times in one evening is clearly owed a fifth and a sixth. Hidenseekk of Stormscale put a pistol ball in him in the Silverwing Flag Room. Apacolyptic of Bleeding Hollow followed with something called Reap the Storm, which a Kul Tiran of all people ought to have seen coming. The Horde took the flag and the field. Nine minutes, start to finish. The Gulch does not do long goodbyes.

He came home to the Bazaar with two more Delver’s Calls in his pocket, Parhelion Plaza and The Darkway, and two new names in the stable ledger: a Ghastly Charger and the Headless Horseman’s own Hallowed Charger. The chronicler asked no questions. It is October in Azeroth. Ghost horses turn up.

Six deaths. Close to eight hundred gold earned and not a copper spent. A new helm, a burnt breastplate, a sword out of a crypt, and one more rung on a ladder that never ends.

And north of Eversong, the Gates of Zul’Aman. The trolls built that road, too. They have been waiting a long time for someone to walk up it.

item.title: Old Scars at Suncrown
item.description: The vines had gotten into Suncrown Village the way rot gets into a ship’s hull: quietly at first, then all at once. They climbed the white stone of the old elven houses and threaded through the gilded railings, thick as mooring line and the wrong color for anything that grows in honest soil. Burrly stood at the edge of the square with the light of Eversong Woods coming gold through the leaves and studied the tendrils the way a Kul Tiran studies a knot somebody else tied badly.
item.content:encoded:
The vines had gotten into Suncrown Village the way rot gets into a ship’s hull: quietly at first, then all at once. They climbed the white stone of the old elven houses and threaded through the gilded railings, thick as mooring line and the wrong color for anything that grows in honest soil. Burrly stood at the edge of the square with the light of Eversong Woods coming gold through the leaves and studied the tendrils the way a Kul Tiran studies a knot somebody else tied badly.

Then he went to work.

He had come up out of Deatholme wearing a dead man’s mask and carrying a question called What’s Left. The chronicler had hoped, briefly, that the answer might require some contemplation. It did not. The answer was a village half-strangled by void-touched growth and a handful of tired elves who needed someone large to start cutting. Choking Tendrils, they called the job, with the blunt honesty of people too exhausted for poetry.

Ten minutes. That is how long the vines held out against a man who learned his trade hauling rigging in a gale. Whatever had been nesting in the growth came at him in ones and twos and left its coin behind in small, steady handfuls, the way a tide leaves driftwood. The chronicler counted the clink of each purse hitting the ground and stopped counting somewhere around the seventh. The work was not glorious. It was a man and an axe and a weed problem with ambitions. Most of the work that saves a town looks exactly like that.

When it was done, he turned in both debts in the same breath: the tendrils cut, and What’s Left answered at last. The elves of Suncrown pressed a cloak into his hands, the Suncrown Savior’s Drape, and he had it over his shoulders before anyone finished thanking him. The chronicler notes that the village named a garment “Savior” before the ink on the job was dry. Quel’Thalas has always been quick with its titles. It is slower with its trust.

Then came Premonition, which took less than half a minute to deliver. A premonition that brief is less a prophecy than a weather report. Whatever was foreseen, it pointed two directions at once: toward Old Scars, and toward something they called A Foe Unseen. Burrly took both. He did not ask which was more dangerous. Warriors rarely do, and the ones who ask tend to get the same answer anyway.

Old Scars asked him to go back out among the ruined edges of the village, where the vines had done their worst. More fighting, more coin. Among the leavings he found a parcel of Bazaar Bites, which is the kind of treasure the world coughs up when it has nothing better to offer: someone’s market-stall supper, carried into a void-blighted forest and never eaten. He also pried loose a weapon called Cre’van’s Punisher and turned it over in his hands long enough to memorize every line of it, the way warriors do with blades they would like to be seen carrying someday. He did not keep the name of Cre’van. Cre’van, presumably, is past caring.

By the time he set Old Scars to rest, his purse was a hundred and forty-odd gold heavier and he had spent not a copper of it. Twenty minutes, start to finish. The Silvermoon Court still counted him a friend. Valeera Sanguinar’s regard sat where it has sat for as long as these pages have existed, at a height that usually means either a life saved or a favor about to be called in.

He made his camp in Eversong Woods with the Drape across his shoulders and one task still unfinished in his ledger.

A Foe Unseen. The vines were the symptom. Something planted them. Something in this golden, wounded forest has been patient enough to grow a weapon one tendril at a time, and it has not shown its face. The chronicler has followed enough adventurers to know that the unseen foe is never unseen for long. It is only waiting to be sure you are worth looking at.

Burrly, it seems, has just made himself worth looking at.

item.title: The Debt That Walks
item.description: The axe had a name: Traitor Captain’s Executioner. Burrly pulled it from the grip of a dead elf who had stopped being a blood elf sometime before he stopped breathing, and the weapon’s purpose was printed right there in the steel. The chronicler appreciates when a tool is honest about its intentions.
item.content:encoded:
The axe had a name: Traitor Captain’s Executioner. Burrly pulled it from the grip of a dead elf who had stopped being a blood elf sometime before he stopped breathing, and the weapon’s purpose was printed right there in the steel. The chronicler appreciates when a tool is honest about its intentions.

“Three battles for Tranquillien,” he had said, accepting the ledger from a clerk whose hands shook. By the time the Kul Tiran walked back through the gates, only one word of that promise remained true: the battles were done. Whether the town still belonged to Tranquillien was a question the void had forced into open debate.

The first fight was straightforward. Cultists had taken positions in the outer ruins, the kind of people who wear too many hoods and speak in sentences that make grammar sound like a suggestion. Burrly went through them like a storm tide through a fishing village. They were not ready for a man who answered their whispered incantations with the kind of silence that comes after an axe connects with a spine. The Heart of Tranquillien, whatever that artifact truly was, returned to its pedestal. The chronicler suspects “heart” is optimistic nomenclature for something that probably beats in the wrong direction.

Then came the traitors. This is where the story loses its shine. The Traitors of Tranquillien wore the same tabards as the guards who had watched Burrly fall through the gates two days prior. He killed them anyway. A Kul Tiran understands duty the way a sailor understands a storm: you do not argue with it, you do not appeal to its mercy, you simply stand where you are supposed to stand and hope the ship holds. He collected their captain’s axe as a receipt. At the inn that night, he strapped a Corrupted Twilight Cowl across his shoulders, the fabric still carrying whatever dark air the traitors had breathed into it. A spare pair of Twilight Spy’s Legguards completed the ensemble. The chronicler notes that Burrly now dresses like the people he just killed, which is either pragmatic scavenging or the opening act of a cautionary tale.

The missing magister turned up. He had been missing in the way that people who fall into void rifts tend to be, which is to say he was found but not all of him. Burrly completed what the magister could not and pocketed a Depleted Voidshard Ring for his trouble. “Depleted” is doing a lot of work in that name. The ring glittered darkly, the way a cave mouth glitters when you are standing too close to it.

And then: the Shadow Enclave. Valeera Sanguinar fell in beside him without a word. She had been Exalted to him since before the chronicler started keeping these records, which in Quel’Thalas means either blood debt or shared secret. Possibly both. The delve descended into a geometry that did not respect itself. Antenorian was waiting at the bottom, a creature whose name sounds like a sneeze and whose presence felt like a migraine gaining theological weight. Burrly and Valeera killed him anyway. A Pledgebearer’s Mask came off the corpse, the kind of headpiece that makes a man look like he has secrets even if he does not. He put it on immediately. Warriors.

The delve spat him back out into the Ruins of Deatholme with gold in his purse and a Primeval Arcane Remnant in his pack, a fragment of something older than the Sundering that the chronicler is frankly not qualified to describe without several more drinks. His mining reached eight. His herbalism reached six. Three hundred and forty thousand gold richer and nine hundred and fifty thousand poorer for the repairs, because the Shadow Enclave does not return equipment in the condition it was lent.

Night found him standing at the edge of Deatholme with a new quest called What’s Left. The answer, so far, appears to be: quite a lot. A magister’s ghost, a void that refuses to stay sealed, and a blood elf rogue who fights beside him for reasons she has not yet seen fit to explain. Burrly logged out still wearing the mask.

The chronicler poured another drink. Whatever walks out of Deatholme tomorrow will not be the same man who walked in. The axe knows. The mask knows. The ring, depleted though it may be, knows most of all.

item.title: The Man Who Fell to Quel’Thalas
item.description: The Kul Tiran hit the ground before he saw the ground. One moment Burrly was crossing into Quel’Thalas; the next, the autumn-gold grass of Eversong Woods was introducing itself to his face with an enthusiasm he had not requested. The chronicler has watched many arrivals in this ancient land. Few have been quite so horizontal.
item.content:encoded:
The Kul Tiran hit the ground before he saw the ground. One moment Burrly was crossing into Quel’Thalas; the next, the autumn-gold grass of Eversong Woods was introducing itself to his face with an enthusiasm he had not requested. The chronicler has watched many arrivals in this ancient land. Few have been quite so horizontal.

Death, here, is a formality. Burrly picked himself up, brushed the loam from his pauldrons, and walked into Tranquillien as though he had meant to do that. Warriors of Kul Tiras are not easily embarrassed, which is fortunate, because the blood elf guards at the gate absolutely saw the whole thing.

Tranquillien is a town with a name that promises peace and a reality that delivers something closer to organized desperation. Burrly arrived to find it teetering. The void has fingers in Eversong now, long and patient, and those fingers were curling around the town’s throat. Five quests fell to him in fifteen minutes: a pace that suggests either extraordinary competence or the kind of urgency that makes quest-givers stop checking credentials. The chronicler suspects both.

He cut through “Appeal to the Void” and “Rational Explanation” with the efficiency of a man who has learned that void cultists are like cockroaches: the first one you see means there are fifty more you have not found yet. A ransacked laboratory yielded an Eversong Chain for his neck and a Girdle of Herbicide for his waist. These are not subtle names. The blood elves were growing something in that lab, and the belt’s very existence suggests it went poorly.

The chronicler notes the factions that took notice. Valeera Sanguinar already holds Burrly in regard that words like “Exalted” only begin to describe; whatever he did for her, the debt runs deep. Six more factions declared themselves Friendly in the span of a breath: the Silvermoon Court, the Amani Tribe, the Hara’ti, the Ritual Sites, and one that calls itself The Singularity. In the politics of Quel’Thalas, “Friendly” means they have decided not to shoot him on sight. The Singularity’s name alone suggests the courtesy may not survive the week.

And then there was Umbric’s Channeling Focus, a trinket pulled from the wreckage. Umbric’s name carries weight in these parts: the void-etched, gravity-bending kind that makes sensible people walk the other way. Burrly strapped it on without hesitation. Kul Tirans and sensible people have never been the same circle on the diagram. He also pocketed an Oathsworn Ring of Might, which is the sort of name that suggests whoever swore the oath is no longer around to collect on it. Burrly did not ask. Warriors rarely do.

His gathering skills ticked upward between battles. Herbalism at four, Mining at six. The man stops to pick flowers and chip ore in the middle of a void incursion. There is either something admirable or something deeply wrong about that. The chronicler has stopped trying to decide which.

By the time he accepted “The Battle for Tranquillien” and its grim companions, “The Traitors of Tranquillien” and “The Heart of Tranquillien,” his purse had grown heavier by over a hundred and seventy gold and the town had placed its fate in the hands of a stranger who arrived by falling on his face. The innkeeper took his coin for a room. The chronicler took his notes.

Three battles remain on his ledger. A town waits. The void, patient as rot, waits too. And somewhere in the Silvermoon Court, Valeera Sanguinar is keeping a tally that has already reached Exalted, which in this world means one of two things: he saved her life, or he is about to be asked to.

item.title: The Blood Elf Problem
item.description: Burrly returned to Eversong Woods with the weary familiarity of a man who knows the blood elves have a problem and that he, for reasons that escape him, has been designated the solution. He is a Kul Tiran warrior, built like a ship’s mast and carrying three hundred and thirty thousand gold, which in the economy of Azeroth means he could buy the problem and the blood elves along with it. He solves their problems anyway. Old habits.
item.content:encoded:
Burrly returned to Eversong Woods with the weary familiarity of a man who knows the blood elves have a problem and that he, for reasons that escape him, has been designated the solution. He is a Kul Tiran warrior, built like a ship’s mast and carrying three hundred and thirty thousand gold, which in the economy of Azeroth means he could buy the problem and the blood elves along with it. He solves their problems anyway. Old habits.

The problem this time was Lightbloom Ath’Ran, a stretch of sacred ground where the flora had gone mad with some unnamed corruption. The blood elves, being blood elves, had not investigated it themselves. The blood elves, being blood elves, had instead waited for a large human to show up and do the investigating for them. Burrly trimmed their lightbloom. Burrly cultivated their curiosities. Burrly sought their truths and delivered their findings to Silvermoon, each step of the chain rewarding him with exactly three hundred nine thousand, eight hundred copper plus whatever small change the game felt like adding. The chronicler stopped counting the gold after the first two payouts. The chronicler has learned that wealth at Burrly’s level is a number that increases for reasons even the player does not fully track.

The silvermoon magister was wayward. The blood elves needed an appeal to the void, which sounded alarming until you realized they meant it literally and had paperwork for it. Burrly accepted every quest put before him with the expression of a man who stopped reading quest text somewhere around level forty and now just clicks “accept” on reflex. The chronicler respects this. There comes a point in every veteran’s career where the story is no longer what the quest-giver says. The story is what happens.

What happened was this: Burrly equipped a Ring of Overgrowth, which the chronicler notes purely because it replaced something he was wearing before and is therefore an upgrade, which in the endgame economy of Azeroth is the only currency that still matters. A green ring. Item level one-twenty. The kind of drop that would make a lesser adventurer weep with joy and made Burrly nod once and move on.

And then came the Cenarion Circle. Or rather, two druids from the Cenarion Circle server who had decided, correctly, that a large Kul Tiran in Eversong Woods was an opportunity for target practice. Morphmious opened with Twin Claw, twenty-six thousand damage in a single blow that left Burrly’s corpse crumpled among the lightbloom like an offering the plants declined to accept. Zalbinoo followed up with Fury of Elune, a spell whose name suggests divine wrath and whose execution suggested someone who had been waiting for this moment all day. Burrly died again. Three thousand six hundred damage. The chronicler notes the numbers because numbers at this level mean something: Morphmious hit like a collapsing cathedral; Zalbinoo finished what was left.

The third death was not PvP. The third death was gravity. Burrly fell in Tranquillien, seventy-five thousand damage from an opponent that has never lost a fight. The chronicler has seen veteran adventurers die to the environment more times than to raid bosses. The ground is undefeated and always will be.

He logged out with eight new faction standings discovered, because at level eighty the game apparently decided he needed to know his reputation with the Ritual Sites, the Hara’ti, the Amani Tribe, the Singularity, the Silvermoon Court, and the Slayer’s Duellum, all of which he discovered by existing in their general vicinity. Valeera Sanguinar, at least, was Exalted. The chronicler does not know what Burrly did to earn Valeera Sanguinar’s eternal devotion and suspects Burrly does not know either.

The quest chain hung unfinished. Appeal to the Void. Rational Explanation. Two threads dangling from a journal that has seen more completed quests than most adventurers will ever accept. He will be back. The blood elves will have another problem. They always do.

item.title: The Eversong Circuit
item.description: The first thing Burrly discovered in Eversong Woods was that Valeera Sanguinar thinks rather highly of him. Exalted, in fact , a word that sits uneasily on a Kul Tiran warrior built more like a dock crane than a diplomat. The chronicler cannot say what history passed between a Blood Elf spymaster and a man who solves problems by walking into them, but the factions of Quel’Thalas have clearly been keeping notes.
item.content:encoded:
The first thing Burrly discovered in Eversong Woods was that Valeera Sanguinar thinks rather highly of him. Exalted, in fact , a word that sits uneasily on a Kul Tiran warrior built more like a dock crane than a diplomat. The chronicler cannot say what history passed between a Blood Elf spymaster and a man who solves problems by walking into them, but the factions of Quel’Thalas have clearly been keeping notes.

Six of them opened their ledgers to him the moment he arrived. The Amani Tribe. The Hara’ti. The Silvermoon Court. The Singularity , which sounds less like a faction and more like a philosophy you’d hear from someone who has read exactly one book and made it their personality. Ritual Sites, which is either a faction or a to-do list. And Slayer’s Duellum, which greeted him with the studied neutrality of people who have seen his type before and are reserving judgment.

Then he got to work.

Burrly does not quest so much as he harvests. The man had his pickaxe and herb satchel out before the innkeeper could finish pretending there were no rooms available. Eversong Woods, for all its autumnal beauty, is practically a geological argument in favor of mining , the kind of place where interesting rocks push up through the soil like they’re trying to escape. He pulled septarian nodules from the earth. He learned things about mining that have names like Dazzling Thorium and Artisan Miner’s Moxie, which sounds like a dwarven drinking song but is apparently a technique. He learned to mine at midnight, which the chronicler chooses to interpret literally.

Then he put the pickaxe down and picked flowers with the same industrial enthusiasm. Herbalism came slower , the plants of Eversong are more subtle than its rocks , but by the time the sun began to think about setting, he had coaxed four ranks of knowledge from the local flora. The chronicler notes, with some amusement, that a man the size of a small ship can identify a Lightbloom at forty paces but still can’t tell you what Quality means in the context of herb gathering.

The quests came in a rhythm. Eversong. Sharpmaw. Fairbreeze Favors. Displaced Denizens. Lightbloom Looming. Each one handed in with the same mechanical certainty, each one paying the same thirty-thousand-odd gold , a sum that would make a younger adventurer weep and which Burrly deposited without breaking stride. His coin purse sits at three hundred thirty million. The chronicler has stopped trying to contextualize these numbers. Suffice to say the man could buy Silvermoon City and still have enough left over to tip poorly.

The gear improved. Lynxslayer’s Reinforced Gauntlets for the hands, Lightstalker’s Greaves for the feet. Both unremarkable items that are nevertheless better than what he had before. That is the quiet tragedy of the endgame: every upgrade is incremental, every victory a rounding error. The chronicler has watched heroes replace their entire armory without once feeling stronger. Burrly, to his credit, does not seem bothered. He is not here to feel strong. He is here to be efficient.

Two quests remain on his slate , Trimming the Lightbloom and Curious Cultivation , when he finally stops. Twenty-seven minutes in Eversong Woods. Forty-four million gold richer, if the chronicler’s arithmetic holds, which it rarely does after the first mug. Mining at rank six. Herbalism at rank four. A Mote of Light in his bag that glows with the smugness of something rare.

The chronicler watched him log out near the Path of Dawn. The name is appropriate. Every road in Quel’Thalas leads somewhere that sounds like a poem. Burrly will be back on it tomorrow, pickaxe in one hand, the other already reaching for the next flower.

item.title: Where the Tide Left Him
item.description: The Waking Shores smelled of ash and promise , the way new continents always do before the cartographers ruin everything with accurate maps. Burrly arrived at Wingrest Embassy with the particular impatience of a man who has sailed through storms and sees no reason a dragon-infested coastline should slow him down. He’s Kul Tiran. They’re built like that.
item.content:encoded:
The Waking Shores smelled of ash and promise , the way new continents always do before the cartographers ruin everything with accurate maps. Burrly arrived at Wingrest Embassy with the particular impatience of a man who has sailed through storms and sees no reason a dragon-infested coastline should slow him down. He’s Kul Tiran. They’re built like that.

The djaradin had awoken, which , the chronicler notes with some fatigue , is what ancient enemies always do the moment fresh adventurers wander into range. Burrly was handed a quest before his boots were dry: Excuse the Mess. The mess, as it turned out, was the djaradin. The excuse was his axe. He got to work.

What followed was the familiar rhythm of a man finding his footing in a strange land. He rescued dragon whelps from the Scalecracker Keep, reported for duty at the Obsidian Citadel, and learned , as all warriors eventually learn in the Dragon Isles , that everything here is on fire and at least half of it wants to kill you. The other half just wants you to fill out paperwork. He did both. Eight quests in thirty-five minutes is not the pace of a tourist. It is the pace of a man who knows the tide waits for no one, not even on a continent suspended in the sky.

Along the way his hands found the old trades: mining and herbalism. He cracked open heated ore deposits and pulled rousing fire from the earth, stuffing the spoils into whatever pockets remained. The chronicler has watched a thousand adventurers gather herbs and ore. None of them look proud doing it. Burrly didn’t either, but he looked competent, which is rarer.

He left the Dragon Isles at level fifteen, which is to say: still small enough that a dragon would need to squint to notice him, but no longer so small that a djaradin could ignore him. Progress of a sort. The ladder extends upward forever, but the first rungs are the only ones that feel anything like flying.

Then , somewhere between the Waking Shores and the Eastern Kingdoms, in the space between logging out and logging back in , Burrly changed. When he reappeared for his second session of the day, he was eighty. Not the slow climb of experience, but the sudden arrival of everything at once: Battle Stance and Defensive Stance, Mortal Strike and Overpower, Heroic Leap, Bladestorm, Colossus Smash , a dozen abilities flooding his muscle memory like a tide coming in. The chronicler has seen this before. The how matters less than the what-next.

The what-next took him to Hammerfall in the Arathi Highlands, where he accepted three writs of Notoriety , with the Vizier, the Weaver, the General , the kind of bureaucratic death warrant that passes for paperwork at level eighty. He abandoned a trading post report and a treasure hunt along the way, which says something about priorities when a man has fifty-two million gold coming and twenty-two minutes to spend it.

A stop in Stormwind. Cathedral Square. A quest called Midnight, accepted with the quiet gravity of a thing whose name sounds less like a task and more like a prophecy. Then the bank: fifty million gold, arriving in a single transaction the way mail from the auction house does when you’ve been away long enough for the market to miss you. He didn’t pause to count it. He bought the tabard of Kul Tiras , the anchor sigil worn across his chest like a second heart , and kept moving.

Stormwind gave way to Silvermoon, the spires of Quel’Thalas rising pink and gold against a sky that has never quite forgiven what happened here. He accepted Eversong. He completed Adventuring in Midnight. He explored the Bazaar, the Sanctum of Light. The city remembered him, or at least its factions did: the Silvermoon Court welcomed him as a friend, and Valeera Sanguinar herself , exalted, which in Blood Elf reckoning probably means she didn’t have him followed. Slayer’s Duellum remained neutral. Some things you earn. Some things you don’t.

Fifty-seven minutes total across two sessions. Three levels gained in the morning, a lifetime of abilities unlocked by afternoon, and enough gold to make a goblin weep into his ledger. Burrly ended the day where the tide left him: Silvermoon City, a tabard on his back and a quest called Eversong still glowing in his log, unanswered, like a question the sun hasn’t risen on yet.

item.title: The Voyage Out
item.description: The gold arrived before the quest did.
item.content:encoded:
The gold arrived before the quest did.

Burrly stood in the Harbormaster’s Office in Boralus , a Kul Tiran warrior with the kind of build that suggests he’s won more arguments with his fists than with his words , when his coin purse suddenly contained five million gold pieces. The chronicler, who has watched adventurers scrape together coppers for decades, set down his quill and stared at the ledger for a long moment. Enough gold to fund a small war. Enough gold to buy a fleet. Enough to make a goblin trade prince develop a nervous twitch.

Burrly did what any sensible man does when suddenly wealthy beyond reason: he went straight to Stormwind and spent nearly half of it before sundown.

The trip was official, at least. “For the Alliance” , the quest-giver said it with the weight of ceremony, and Burrly, who understands that paperwork is the true endgame of every hero’s journey, accepted without comment. He crossed the sea, presented himself at the Stormwind Embassy, and was handed a Tabard of Kul Tiras as if the anchor on his chest needed official recognition. He put it on immediately. A man doesn’t forget where he came from, even when his pockets say he never has to go back.

Then the spending began. Six bank tabs purchased in rapid, mechanical succession , the “Safer Deposit” achievement, as though anyone in Azeroth has ever felt safe about anything stored in a bank. Sunfire Silk Backpacks, four of them, bought like a man who expects to fill every one. An Arcanoweave Reagent Rucksack for good measure. Half a million gold on bank tabs alone. The goblin clerks, creatures not known for their emotional range, looked genuinely moved.

With the banking sorted , because even a warrior headed for the Dragon Isles needs somewhere to keep his rocks , Burrly turned to the practical arts. He learned to mine, cracking open the earth with the same enthusiasm he brings to cracking skulls. Smelt Copper: the first recipe every aspiring smith learns and immediately forgets exists once better ores present themselves. He learned to gather herbs. And he learned to fish, because whatever else a Kul Tiran becomes , warrior, wanderer, suddenly-wealthy eccentric , he is first and always a man of the sea.

The journey to the Dragon Isles proceeded with the grim efficiency of bureaucracy. “The Dragon Isles Await.” “Aspectral Invitation.” “Whispers on the Winds.” Quest after quest of people telling Burrly things he already knew, in rooms he’d already visited, about threats he’d already agreed to face. The chronicler has watched a thousand heroes run this same gauntlet. None of them have ever looked happy about it.

Then, at last, the ship. The Wild Coast materializing out of the ocean mist. The Waking Shores spreading before him , volcanic, primordial, a land that had been sleeping since before the Sundering and was still blinking awake. The chronicler will say this for the Dragon Isles: they know how to make an entrance.

Burrly learned to climb. The world , and here the chronicler means the strange metaphysics that govern this realm , taught him to detect anomalies and bypass mechanisms, skills his people traditionally addressed by hitting things until they stopped being problems. Progress, of a sort. He also learned to fish again, because the Dragon Isles are very particular about fishing credentials. Two different fishing instructors had to sign off. The sea, apparently, has standards now.

The first creatures fell to Mortal Strike. A Chitin Dreadbringer dropped from something with too many legs, and Burrly picked it up, tested its weight, and kept walking. Warriors who pause to admire their weapons rarely live to use them twice. He learned Berserker Rage at level twelve , which is exactly what it sounds like and exactly what you want a man of his size to bring to a fight.

Two level-ups in forty-two minutes. The chronicler notes this without judgment. Some days, the world simply yields.

He abandoned one quest. Something about lava beetles and artisan supplies. A man with nearly three million gold remaining in his pockets can afford to be selective. The beetles, one assumes, will find another supplier.

By the time Burrly reached the Wingrest Embassy, the sun had set and his quest log held more open threads than a goblin’s ledger: Wrathion was missing, elementals were encroaching, someone needed quality assurance, and a frankly inexplicable quest about a bar tab barrel had been completed , a task so absurd the chronicler suspects it was written while drunk and accepted under the same condition.

He logged out in the Waking Shores. Twelve levels. Three professions. A rare blade on his back. Gold enough to make a dragon consider early retirement. The chronicler poured another drink and watched the embers settle in the hearth. Some heroes claw their way to fortune inch by bloody inch, copper by grudging copper. Others arrive with it already in their pockets, as if the universe had placed a bet and was waiting to see if it paid off.

The Dragon Isles await. Wrathion is missing. The beetles, for now, are someone else’s problem.

item.title: The Man Who Knew Everyone
item.description: The Harbormaster’s Office in Boralus smells of salt, fish, and paperwork , three things the sea has never learned to separate. Burrly stood in its doorway, a Kul Tiran on Kul Tiran soil, and the world rushed to greet him like a debtor greeting a creditor. Seven factions introduced themselves before he’d taken three steps. Some of them he’d never met. One of them, a blood elf named Valeera Sanguinar, apparently considers him family. The chronicler has stopped trying to explain these things.
item.content:encoded:
The Harbormaster’s Office in Boralus smells of salt, fish, and paperwork , three things the sea has never learned to separate. Burrly stood in its doorway, a Kul Tiran on Kul Tiran soil, and the world rushed to greet him like a debtor greeting a creditor. Seven factions introduced themselves before he’d taken three steps. Some of them he’d never met. One of them, a blood elf named Valeera Sanguinar, apparently considers him family. The chronicler has stopped trying to explain these things.

He is a warrior. That much is clear from the breadth of his shoulders , Kul Tirans are built like the ships they sail, and Burrly is no exception. What is less clear is why a man who just arrived in his own homeland already carries the goodwill of the Amani Tribe, the Silvermoon Court, and something called The Singularity, which sounds less like a faction and more like a theological crisis. The Warband’s shadow is long, and it touches everyone who walks in its wake. Burrly is level ten and already the world owes him favors he did not earn. The chronicler takes no position on whether this is a blessing or a debt that will come due later. Probably both.

The first thing he learned was Second Wind , a warrior’s gift, the body’s stubborn refusal to quit when quitting would be simpler. It suits him. It suits every Kul Tiran who ever sailed through a storm and pretended afterward that it wasn’t that bad.

Then the Warband’s tools arrived: a map to everywhere, all at once, and some kind of bank inhibitor that lets him reach into a vault from anywhere in the world. Practical magic, the sort that saves you the walk back to Orgrimmar or Stormwind. The chronicler remembers when adventurers carried everything they owned on their backs and liked it. The chronicler is also old and has been wrong about most things.

Twenty-six minutes. That was the whole of it. He stood in Boralus Harbor, learned to shift between Battle Stance and Defensive Stance , the warrior’s eternal conversation with himself: hit harder, or get hit less. These are the only two sentences a warrior ever needs, and everything else is punctuation.

He learned Defensive Stance first, which tells you something about the man. Battle Stance came second. The chronicler notes these things. A warrior who learns to protect before he learns to swing is either a natural leader or a natural target, and the line between the two is thinner than most would like to admit.

The Slayer’s Duellum regarded him with neutrality , the one faction that did not fall over itself to welcome him. They will come around. Or they will not. Factions are like tides: predictable in pattern, unpredictable in timing, and utterly indifferent to your opinion of them.

He logged out still standing in the harbor, the salt air clinging to his tunic, his quest log empty and his path unwritten. A Kul Tiran at level ten with the weight of a Warband behind him and not a single scar to show for it. That will change. The chronicler has seen enough warriors to know that the quiet ones, the ones who stand in harbors and learn to defend before they attack, are the ones whose names end up in songs. Or on gravestones. The chronicler does not write the endings , only the chapters.

The tide is coming in. Boralus waits. And somewhere, Valeera Sanguinar is apparently preparing a guest room.

item.title: Picking a main … Forever
item.description: I’ve played a little bit of most of my favorite classes on World of Warcraft Forever, and I’m trying to decide what to main. Somehow it always comes back to Paladin. Personality-wise it just fits me best. I do love mages, mostly for the teleports, because who doesn’t want to skip the boat ride? But I think pally is going to be my thing.
item.content:encoded:
I’ve played a little bit of most of my favorite classes on World of Warcraft Forever, and I’m trying to decide what to main. Somehow it always comes back to Paladin. Personality-wise it just fits me best. I do love mages, mostly for the teleports, because who doesn’t want to skip the boat ride? But I think pally is going to be my thing.

I’m an ex-soldier and a Baha’i, which puts me in a funny spot: I enjoy a good fight, but what I really want is peace and unity. It’s a great contradiction. A Paladin covers both. Hit things with a hammer, then heal everyone afterward.

And let’s not forget the Horde side. My goodness, what a redemption story Forsaken Paladins have! Undead turning back to the Light is better than any 80s comeback montage. I’ll probably play a Forsaken on the PvP phase and a Human for PvE, so I get to see both sides. Once those two hit sixty and are decently geared, I’ll think about leveling that mage. A man can only resist free teleports for so long.

What are y’all planning to play?

item.title: Welcome to My Azeroth Life
item.description: Hi. Hello. Is this thing still on?
item.content:encoded:
Hi. Hello. Is this thing still on?

This is a reboot of sorts. I used to own this domain and ran a little blog on it. It never went far. Then the domain quietly expired, like a Tamagotchi I forgot to feed. I’m honestly surprised nobody grabbed it while I was gone. Hard to believe the internet didn’t snap it up, but here we are, together again, like a band’s reunion tour nobody asked for.

Then Blizzard announced World of Warcraft: Forever, and it felt like a sign. Everything’s new, and on November 4th everyone starts from zero at the same time. No head starts and no gear gap. It’s just all of us standing in a starting zone, looking at the quest givers and wondering who has the exclamation point. I can’t think of a better time to start over. Full disclosure: I’ve already been poking around in the beta, so I may have a map or two folded in my back pocket.

I’ll probably still wander into retail and other WoW topics now and then. Old habits and all that. Mostly, though, I expect I’ll be living in Forever for a good long while.

So grab a log and pull up a spot by the campfire. Stick around while I ramble about grand adventures in a reborn Azeroth. I promise the stories get better than this one. Probably.

Cheers!
